blocks.text: Forty starlings went into the Sedgeway crate at noon. I checked every leg ring and counted every bird myself, twice, because that is the job, and because nobody else at the Circuit Loft counts twice.
At ten past four, over Hobsmere Reedbed, with Hobsmere Cutters at the bottom of the table and one bad night from the bottom of the world, I put my loft glass on the same flock and counted forty-one.
I counted again. Forty-one.
I am not good at much. I am good at numbers, and I am good at birds, and until that afternoon the two had always agreed with each other.

The crate van left Wenlode at one o'clock. It carried two crates, Sedgeway and Mallow, strapped side by side under a tarpaulin that smelled of creosote and seed. The lot at the Loose would say which one flew. The other would ride home unopened and be cross about it. Starlings are always cross about something. I sat between the crates on an upturned feed bin with my knee against the Sedgeway door, because Sedgeway birds settle quicker when they can hear someone breathing who isn't a hawk.
Amos Thurlow drove. Amos is the senior loft-man after the loft-master, and he does not like me in his cab, so I rode in the back. That suited both of us.

I was the Loft's spare hand. I had been the spare hand for three winters. When a loft-man was ill, I went. When a loft-man was not ill but did not fancy Hobsmere in January, I went. I fed six flocks, scraped six lofts, ringed the young birds every summer and counted the old ones every morning. Nobody had ever asked for me by name. That Saturday I wanted to keep it that way for one more afternoon: open the crate, stand at the reed-line, recall any birds that strayed before roost-light, crate the rest after full dark, and go home.
Hobsmere is a reed-cutters' village at the end of a causeway. Hobsmere Mere lies along one long side of the Reedbed, grey and flat as a slate roof, and the Wenlode road goes the long way round it.

A grey heron lifted off the dyke as we came down the causeway. Then two moorhens. Then Wilfred Cobbing, the Cutters' chairman, came out of the Dyke Arms with a half-made eel trap under his arm and asked Amos whether we had brought them a kind flock.
"Flocks don't come kind," Amos said.
"No," said Mr Cobbing. "Nor does Brindwater."
Hobsmere had ten points from twelve matches. Everyone in the Marsh Circuit knew it, including the reeds.

The light was the colour of dishwater by half past three. At the Ringing, through the open door of the clubhouse, I watched Hamish Toller close six copper rings on six wrists, his own last, and hold out his hand so Lucas Mbeki could take the withy from it. Lucas took it carefully, as though it might be wound too tight. Hamish said something that made Rhys Dorne laugh. Joan Pettifer did not laugh. Joan was looking at the sky the way a drainage engineer looks at a sluice gate, waiting for it to fail.
At four o'clock a counter drew a wooden token out of a bag at centre and held it up. Sedgeway.

I unstrapped the crate. I counted them out as they went: a clatter of wings at the door, then the long pour of them up into the grey, each one a dark comma, each one a number. Thirty-eight, thirty-nine, forty. The crate was empty. The flock was forty. I wrote it in my book.
Hamish raised before the last bird had cleared the reeds.

I should say here that I can see shades. I always have. The Loft's pamphlet says one person in several thousand can, and the Loft has never asked, because the Loft wants its birds counted, not its hands examined. I have never offered. A spare hand who sees things is still a spare hand.

So I saw the six Hobsmere shades go up together, six bird-shapes at Hamish's ceiling, each flying directly over the head of its wearer and moving as he moved. Over Rhys, sprinting along the near reed-line with his elbows going and his own commentary going with them: "And Dorne takes the reed-line, and the crowd cannot believe its luck." Over Kit Bunyard on the far side. Over Joan and Mercy Ledbetter at the back, reading Hamish's hands. Over Lucas, already jogging towards the Brindwater Roost. Over Hamish himself, last, a little higher than the rest, as if his own shade had to keep an eye on the others.
Brindwater's Wing raised six of her own a breath later. She was a tall woman in a green scarf, and she did not hurry.

Hamish herded. That is what most Wings do: spread the shades along one edge of the flock so every bird on that edge has one or two strange neighbours among its seven, and leans a little, and the flock leans with it. Brindwater's Wing put her ceiling on Hamish's ceiling and laid her shades along the same edge, shade for shade, and every lean he gave the birds she took back. Nobody on the ground saw any of this. The crowd on the bank saw forty starlings and twelve people running about in the mud.
I saw it. I also saw that she was faster.

At ten past four the flock came low over the centre reed-line, close enough that I could hear it, that soft tearing sound a flock makes, like someone ripping a sheet a long way off. I lifted my glass out of habit. A loft hand counts.
Thirty-nine, forty, forty-one.
I lowered the glass. I raised it. I counted from the other edge, slower, the way I count a young flock that won't keep still.
Forty-one.

I knew where every shade was. Twelve of them, each above its runner, each at its Wing's ceiling. I had not counted those. This was something else. It flew inside the flock's near edge, at the flock's height, turning when the flock turned, nobody beneath it but reeds. Starlings were sitting on either side of it and steering by it as if it belonged there.
The flock tilted and the bird tilted with it, and for perhaps a second I had its leg in the glass.

It wore a ring. Not a Loft ring. A copper band, like the rings Hamish had closed in the clubhouse, like the rings that show on a shade's leg. A player's ring. But where a ring this season says CCIII, this one had a single upright stroke. One numeral. I. The number after it had worn away to nothing, the way the step of an old church wears away.
Season I.
"Forty-one," I said.
I said it aloud. I didn't mean to. It is what I say at the Loft every morning, the number, out loud, so the loft-master can write it down.
Beside me at the crate stand, the counter flinched.

She was a small woman in a long oilskin with a counter's brass badge on the collar and a match sheet clipped to a board. Her name was Dorcas Ely; it was on the sheet. She did not look up at the flock. She looked at her board. Her pencil moved.
"Forty, miss," she said.
"There are forty-one," I said. "There's one on the near edge, with a—"
"Forty, miss." Quieter. She was writing it as she said it, a four and a nought, very neat. "You'll want to watch your strays."
Twenty paces along the reed-line, Joan Pettifer turned her head and looked at me. She had come back to read Hamish's hands and had heard me instead. Then Hamish signalled, and she ran.
I watched my strays.

There were none, at first. Sedgeway is a sensible flock. It went where the shades leaned it, and the shades leaned it towards Hobsmere's Roost, because Brindwater's Wing kept taking Hamish's edge away from him and giving it back pointed the wrong way. Hamish's hands went faster. He changed his ceiling twice, and each time his shades hung back for a full breath while they found the new height, and Brindwater's were already waiting there for him. That is ceiling-sniping. It's legal, and it was working.

I kept the glass on the forty-first bird. It kept to the edge. Once it drifted up the flock towards Hamish's own shade, close, and I lost it against the grey, and when I found it again it was back at the edge where it started. Hamish's hands stopped for half a second. Then they went on.

At twenty minutes past four the counters called the Breath. Hamish dropped all six shades and stood with his hands open for one full minute while the counter at the far Roost timed it on a watch. Brindwater did not have to drop anything. Their shades leaned the flock another ten yards towards Hobsmere's end.
Hamish raised again at twenty-one minutes past, and did not stop.

At half past four the counters declared roost-light. The light had gone the colour of pewter, and the reeds had stopped casting shadows. Dorcas Ely called the counted flock in a clear voice, for the bank to hear.
"Forty."
Every ringed bird still with the flock. I had lost none. And a forty-first was flying with it, keeping its edge, and nobody counted it because it was not anyone's to count.

The Settle is when the doors matter. Brindwater's Reed was already at Hobsmere's Roost, working the mouth of it. Brindwater's Wing stopped herding and brought her shades in close along the flock's leading edge, three on one side of the point bird, three on the other. The point bird leaned. The flock leaned with it, because it was already leaning that way. That is the whole art, Amos says. Never push a flock. Find where it's going and get there first.

Hamish called long. He was chasing the settle with everything he had. Twenty minutes after the first Breath, at nineteen minutes to five by my watch, the counters called it again, and he dropped and stood his minute, and the flock spilled towards his own Roost the whole time.
He raised again at eighteen minutes to five. I don't think he needed to. I think he could not stop.

Full dark came at ten to five. It always comes all at once in the Fen in winter; one moment there is a flock, and the next there is a sound where the flock was. The counters blew. I looked for the forty-first bird and the sky had nothing in it. I hadn't seen it leave.
The counters counted both Roosts with lanterns. Twenty-four Sedgeway birds in Hobsmere's Roost. Nine in Brindwater's. Seven still on the reeds and the wind, for the loft-men to recall.
Twenty-four of forty is more than half. Partial settle to Brindwater: two points to nothing. The bank went quiet in the way a bank does when it was already expecting it.

I recalled seven birds and crated them, and then went round both Roosts with Amos and crated the rest. While I worked, the counters cut the rings, one counter to each wrist, a pair of shears and a small dull click. Dorcas Ely read Hamish's call off her sheet.
"Forty-eight call-minutes, Mr Toller. Thirty-eight drift."
"I know," said Hamish.
Thirty-eight minutes is a long walk-down. Lucas would have to hold his hand and talk to him for every one of them, and if he let go, they would start again from the first minute.
Joan stood at the reed-line with the rest of them round her and did her arithmetic out loud. I could hear it from the van.

"Where are we? Bottom. Ten points. Tarrow Dyke on fifteen, Pashley Carr on thirteen, five matches to play. Five points from safety, is it? It is. And if we lose again, what do we need? We need to win everything left and have Tarrow and Pashley Carr fall over in the same week. Don't we?"
Nobody answered. Rhys said, "I'll have a word with Tarrow, Joanie. Tell them to mind the stairs."
Nobody laughed at that either.

Hamish's drift had already turned him. I could see it in the way he stood, not facing his crew, not facing the clubhouse, but out across the mere. A Wing's drift doesn't point at the birds. It points where the birds are going home, and the Sedgeway flock was going home to Wenlode. The road to Wenlode goes round Hobsmere Mere. A straight line goes across it.
Lucas took Hamish's hand. I heard him start. Lucas talks like a clock being explained, very precisely, every part in its place.
"Hamish. It's Lucas. W-walk with me. Left foot. The bank path, please, not the reeds. Thirty-eight minutes, and it is, I am told, a perfectly ordinary evening."

They walked. The bank path runs along the mere's edge between the reeds and the water, and they went along it at an old man's pace, Lucas on the water side, talking. Hamish's body went where Lucas walked it. Hamish's face went where the drift went: across the water.

I lifted another crate into the van. Amos lit his pipe. The crowd went home. Joan stayed on the bank with her arms folded and watched them the whole way, and Rhys and Kit stayed with Joan, and Mercy sat on the clubhouse step.
At about twenty minutes in, Lucas stopped talking.

I noticed the silence before I noticed anything else. Then I saw that he had stopped walking too. He was standing on the bank path with Hamish's hand still in his, and he was not looking at Hamish. He was looking where Hamish was looking. Out over the water. There was nothing out there to see. Full dark had come and gone. There was mere, and more mere, and the lights of the Wenlode road a long way round it.
Lucas's hand opened.
Hamish walked into Hobsmere Mere.

He did not hurry. That was the worst of it. He walked the way you'd walk up a garden path. He went in to the knee, and then to the waist, and the cold should have stopped him and didn't, because a drifting Wing does not stop for cold.
"Hamish!" That was Joan. She was at the very edge of the bank. She had her arms out. She did not go in.

Rhys went in. He went in the way he does everything, all at once and shouting. Kit went in behind him. The water was at Hamish's chest when they reached him, and then over his head, and then Rhys had him by the collar and Kit had him by the belt and they were dragging him back the way he'd come, and he was fighting them, not hard, just steadily, the way a bird held in the hand keeps trying the same direction.

They got him onto the bank. He was coughing. He was alive. Restraint holds the body. It doesn't hold the direction. Even lying in the mud with Rhys kneeling on his coat, his face was turned out across the water.
Lucas was on his knees beside him. He took Hamish's hand again. His own hand was shaking.
"I'm sorry," he said. "I'm sorry. W-we're starting again. Minute one."

Thirty-eight more minutes, on the bank, in wet clothes, in January. Mercy ran for the telephone box by the Dyke Arms. Mr Cobbing came out with blankets. Joan stood at the edge of the water where she had stood the whole time, and her arms were still out a little from her sides, as if she had forgotten them.
I stood at the back of the van with a crate of starlings in my arms and did not understand what I had seen.

A tether doesn't stop. That is the one thing a tether is for. And there had been nothing different about tonight. No hawk. No wind. Nothing on the water. He had simply stopped, and turned his head, and looked at the mere as if somebody out there had said his name.

The ambulance came down the causeway at a quarter to seven with its bell going. By then Lucas had walked Hamish down, all thirty-eight minutes, on his knees in the mud. They put Hamish in the back under two grey blankets. Someone said the sanatorium. Someone said pneumonia. Someone said he would not fly again this season, and nobody argued.
Amos started the van. "Get in," he said. "Front."
It was the first time he had ever asked me into the cab. I sat with my hands between my knees and didn't say anything, and neither did he, all the way round the long side of the mere.

At the Circuit Loft I uncrated Sedgeway into its own loft by lamplight and counted them in. A grey wagtail was asleep on the gutter over the door; it did not wake. The starlings went in one by one, cross, cold, ruffled, home.
Forty.
Forty out of the crate at four o'clock. Forty counted at roost-light. Forty back in the loft at eight. Every ring a Loft ring. Every ring a number I had written down myself.

The counters' copy of the match sheet comes home with the flock, for the flight book. Amos had left it on the bench. I read it under the lamp. Released: forty. Counted at roost-light: forty. Settle: Brindwater, partial, twenty-four of forty. Signed in a small, neat hand. D. Ely.

I sat on the feed bin and went back over it the way I go over a count that won't come right. Not the arithmetic. The leg. I had it in the glass for about a second. A copper band, worn thin. A single upright stroke where the season should be. Season I. The league counts one season a year, and this is Season CCIII. That ring had been closed two hundred and two years ago. Nobody alive had seen a ring closed in Season I. Nobody's great-grandmother had.
Nobody should have been wearing it.
And it had been flying over Hobsmere Reedbed at ten past four this afternoon, at the flock's height, with starlings steering by it on either side, and I had said the number out loud.

I thought about Dorcas Ely. She had not looked up when I said it. She hadn't needed to. She had flinched before I finished the word, the way you flinch at a sound you have been waiting for, and her pencil had already been moving.
She had seen it. She had seen a bird two hundred years old over Hobsmere, and she had written forty.
